explanations.explanation: It detects and signals boilerplate legal header text—especially standard open‐source copyright and license declarations (like Apache License v2 boilerplate with its disclaimers and permission language).
It identifies formal legal-document language—triggering on structured citation markers like docket numbers, court names, case designations, and procedural phrasing found in legal texts.

It appears this feature activates for text that fits the formal, templated language of legal documents—sections like case headings and citation lines, docket numbers, and standardized publication or copyright instructions (for example “DO NOT PUBLISH” or “UNPUBLISHED”). In other words, it signals boilerplate legal metadata and formatting typical of court opinions, legal filings, and licensing notices.

It appears that this feature specializes in detecting relational “glue” words—often prepositions or conjunctions such as those in phrases like “apart from” or “since”—that mark a shift or qualification in discourse (for example, signaling exceptions, contrasts, or specifying non‐core, supplementary material).

This feature seems to signal “technical Q&A language” – it activates strongly on text that has the hallmarks of programming or developer troubleshooting questions. In other words, it identifies passages written in the style of technical inquiry (with code snippets, error messages, configuration details, and explicit Q/A formats) as commonly seen on developer forums like Stack Overflow.

It appears that this feature “lights up” on pieces of text that contain non‐standard or accented letter forms—substrings typical of proper names or culturally marked words (for example, the Spanish “ñ” in “mañana” or accented fragments in names like “McGuire”) that signal non‐generic, language‐specific orthography. In short, the feature seems to represent a subcomponent that detects the presence of diacritical or non–plain‐ASCII morphemes commonly found in proper names and other culturally specific tokens.

This feature activates on tokens that form part of structured, formatted numeric information—especially dates, timestamps, version numbers, and similar log‐ or data record–style numeric sequences. In context, high activations occur on tokens marking years, specific date/time strings, and other numeric identifiers embedded in system logs, publication details, URL components, and even math expressions, suggesting the feature signals when the model encounters reliably formatted temporal/numeric metadata.

This feature appears to capture domain‐specific abbreviations and shorthand notations in biomedical and technical texts. In each example, the highest activations occur on multi‐token, often all‐capital letter sequences (or combinations of letters and numbers) that serve as condensed labels for complex entities (e.g. viruses, assays, treatments, devices, or hormones). In short, it signals when the model processes domain-specific acronyms and compound abbreviations that are common in scientific literature.

This feature identifies and “lights up” on alphanumeric tokens that incorporate hyphens—patterns typical of version numbers, model or product identifiers (e.g. “F‑35,” “X‑Mas,” “B‑Series”), and other technical or code-specific string expressions (such as regex ranges or hyphenated parameter names). In essence, it’s detecting the syntactic structure where a dash links letters and/or digits to signal specialized identifiers or version-like labels in technical text.

The feature fires on tokens that mark a “boundary” or shift in text style—points where the text is being formally or visually demarcated (for example through emphasis markers, specialized punctuation, or operator symbols). In other words, it picks out tokens used to signal that a segment of text is formatted or structured (as in markdown‐style emphasis, legal citations, math expressions, or listed items), suggesting a switch in discourse or presentation mode.

It seems that this feature “lights up” on unusual subword pieces that typically begin or mark out multi‐word, “exotic” names and technical terms—that is, it is activated whenever the tokenization hits the head (or a marked part) of a proper noun or compound technical entity (whether a plant name, a geographic/brand name, a chemical/drug term, etc.) that does not occur in ordinary language. In short, the feature appears to signal the presence of distinctive, often hyphenated or multi‐token, name‐ or term–boundaries that carry unique semantic identity.

It appears that this feature fires when the text functions as a header or “about‐section” marker—that is, when a word like “About” (or a similar preposition that signals a transition into descriptive, meta‐information or topic summaries) is used to introduce a block of content (as in navigation labels, section headings, title attributions, or topic introductions).

It appears to be a feature that “lights up” when the text introduces or reinforces a factual or evidential claim – in other words, it activates on discourse markers (like “in fact” or “notably”) that signal emphasis, confirmation, or the presentation of a core fact.

It appears that this feature is sensitive to a specific subword‐fragment—centered on the “om” (or similar) morpheme—that frequently appears in “boilerplate” or structured text. In many examples (from metadata lines like “NOT RECOMMENDED FOR FULL‐TEXT PUBLICATION” to fragments in code or legal filings), the model gives the highest activation to a short mid‐word sequence (e.g. “OM” in “RECOMMENDED”), suggesting that it has specialized in detecting this recurring orthographic unit used in formal, patterned or technical documents.

It appears that this feature “lights‐up” when the model is processing tokens that mark off structured, proper‑noun–like or formatted elements—such as names, titles, identifiers, legal or organizational citations, and other metadata tokens (often in atypical capitalization or with special punctuation) that signal a discrete, formally defined entity in the text.

It appears that this feature is sensitive to content with a technical, algorithm‐oriented style—identifying passages that mix formal mathematical problem statements (for example, computing greatest common divisors or combinatorial probabilities) with structured code syntax (like package declarations and import statements in Java). In essence, it signals text that is set in a technical, programming/math context.

It appears that this feature fires strongly on tokens that serve as formal, structured identifiers or markers—such as citation keys, reference numbers, and section codes—that signal bibliographic or document‐metadata information in technical and academic texts.

It appears that this feature is attuned to recognizing structured header and metadata blocks—such as file encoding settings, copyright and licensing boilerplate, and other formatted document parameters—that show up in code comments and legal text.

It appears that this feature is particularly sensitive to common word‐ending segments—morphemic suffixes or subword fragments (like “‑ger”, “‑ging”, “‑asing”, “‑cient”, “‑itor”, “‑anted”, “‑usion”, “‑ity”, “‑ies”, “‑ental”, etc.) that often signal action, quality, or agentive roles. In other words, it picks up on the morphological endings that mark process, description, or state across diverse contexts (from technical jargon to everyday language) and helps the model recognize and link words with similar semantic functions.

This feature activates on text that exhibits structured, schema‐like data—typically key–value configurations and metadata (in JSON, XML, etc.)—used to specify assets, versions, dependencies, settings, and other technical parameters in software and web contexts.
